paragraphs.heading: What naturalism teaches
paragraphs.edited: You can probably tell right out of the gate that the idea of naturalism has the idea of nature in it. Think of your senses. Think of the five senses that you have — what you can taste, touch, smell, and feel. Naturalism teaches that only those things are what constitutes reality, and there we're back to that word again. What is reality? When we're talking about these other worldviews, they're doing the same thing that we're trying to do: trying to talk about what is reality and what is truth. How do we interpret these things in light of what naturalism actually is? Those who believe in naturalism are trying to take the five senses and interpret reality and dictate what is true based on those factors. That's essentially what they're doing.

paragraphs.heading: Why naturalism can't work
paragraphs.edited: But what I want you to get is that this lesson is more than just understanding what naturalism is. It's being able to see that it can't work. And what we want our students to be able to determine is that they're not going to get away from it, because it's the dominant view of Western culture — but to be able to see things through it and interpret things in light of it, and to understand that naturalism might be trying to do these things, and might be trying to explain meaning through science and the natural world, the natural order of things and all that, but at the end of the day it doesn't really work. Why?

paragraphs.edited: Well, because naturalism is most closely associated with the idea of atheism, which means no God, it cannot explain two fundamental questions. It can't explain the universe in terms of how, and it can't explain things in terms of why. Now, science is trying to do this. Science is trying to figure out how the universe was created, and how things got here, and how it is that we're all here. But science can't do this. It can't determine why. Is it just random? If it's random, why is it random? We could keep asking that why question over and over and over again.

paragraphs.heading: In your small groups
paragraphs.edited: So in your small groups — especially in your small groups — make sure you take the time to allow students to discover and discuss how naturalism manifests itself in Western culture. What does that look like? Where do they see that in their schools and in their classes? It's not just evolutionary science and those kinds of things; it might be deeper than that. So get your students to have those discussions and get them to see beyond just the surface of what naturalism is, and have them start to analyze it in terms of reality and truth.

paragraphs.heading: Ecclesiastes and meaninglessness
paragraphs.edited: One thing that's great about this Bible study is that we dive into Ecclesiastes and the things that Solomon wrote. I think he had this spot on, and it brings so much more to the surface when we consider this book in light of naturalism. He writes in the very, very beginning, right out of the gate: "Meaningless, meaningless, says the teacher, utterly meaningless. Everything is meaningless. What does man gain from all his labor at which he toils under the sun? Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." And what he's getting at through this whole book is the idea that without God putting meaning in life, life is meaningless — that all of our work and all of our efforts and everything that we stand for is meaningless.

paragraphs.heading: The buffet of worldviews
paragraphs.edited: So we see so clearly — and I want your students to see this as well — that when we talk about naturalism, it might sound so easy and so simple. When we talk about that big buffet of worldviews, it might sound like, "Oh yeah, this idea works really well." But when they go down that buffet and they decide that, yeah, I believe in naturalism and I don't believe in God, but I believe in taking care of orphans and widows and providing clean water to children around the world who don't have it — those two things are now inconsistent. Those two things no longer make sense together. It's a great thing that you want to provide that for those people, but why do you want to do that?
